mcq.q: A chemical factory discharges waste into a river and harms fishermen downstream without compensating them. This is an example of a:
mcq.explain: An externality is a cost or benefit falling on third parties who are not part of the transaction. Here the factory's production imposes costs on fishermen, so it is a negative production externality. The social cost of the factory's output exceeds its private cost, so the market overproduces it.
mcq.topic: Externalities — private cost and social cost
mcq.fast: Harm to outsiders from production = negative production externality.

mcq.q: When a person gets vaccinated, others around him are also less likely to catch the disease. This is a:
mcq.explain: Vaccination benefits not only the person vaccinated but also others, who face a lower risk of infection. This spill-over benefit is a positive externality. Because private buyers ignore the benefit to others, the market tends to under-supply such goods, which justifies subsidies or free provision.
mcq.topic: Externalities — private cost and social cost

mcq.q: A city's festival fireworks can be watched by everyone in the area, nobody can be stopped from watching, and one more viewer does not reduce anyone else's enjoyment. Economically, the display is:
mcq.explain: The display is non-excludable, because viewers cannot be prevented from watching, and non-rival, because one more viewer does not reduce what others get. Goods with both features are pure public goods, which markets under-provide because of free riders. A common access resource is rival, and a private good is both rival and excludable.
mcq.topic: Public goods and the free-rider problem

mcq.q: Fishing grounds in the open sea are used by everyone and gradually get over-fished. This illustrates:
options: The tragedy of the commons for a common access resource
mcq.explain: Open-sea fisheries are non-excludable (anyone can fish) but rival (fish caught by one are not available to others). Each user ignores the effect of his catch on others, so the resource is over-used and depleted — the tragedy of the commons. This is a common access resource, not a pure public good.
mcq.topic: Public goods and the free-rider problem

mcq.q: After buying comprehensive vehicle insurance, a driver starts parking carelessly in unsafe places. This is an example of:
options: Free riding on a public good
mcq.explain: Moral hazard arises after a contract is made, when one party changes behaviour because it no longer bears the full cost of its actions. Being insured, the driver takes less care. Adverse selection arises before the contract, when the party with hidden information is more likely to enter it.
mcq.topic: Incomplete information — adverse selection and moral hazard
mcq.fast: Behaviour changes AFTER the deal = moral hazard; hidden info BEFORE = adverse selection.

mcq.q: In a used-car market, buyers cannot tell good cars from bad ones, so good cars are withdrawn and mostly poor-quality cars are left for sale. This is:
options: Adverse selection due to asymmetric information
mcq.explain: When sellers know more about quality than buyers, buyers offer only an average price. Owners of good cars find this too low and withdraw, so the market is left mostly with poor-quality cars ("lemons"). This is adverse selection arising from asymmetric information before the transaction.
mcq.topic: Incomplete information — adverse selection and moral hazard
mcq.fast: Hidden quality before the sale = adverse selection.

mcq.q: A tax levied on a polluting firm equal to the external cost of its pollution is called a:
mcq.explain: A Pigouvian tax, named after A. C. Pigou, is set equal to the marginal external cost of an activity. It makes the polluter bear the full social cost, raising the price of the product and reducing output towards the socially efficient level.

mcq.q: Education and health care are often subsidised by governments because they are:
options: Pure public goods in every case
Merit goods that people tend to under-consume
mcq.explain: Merit goods are goods whose benefits to the individual and to society are greater than people realise, so they would be under-consumed if left to the market. Governments therefore subsidise or provide them free. Demerit goods, such as tobacco, are over-consumed and are taxed or restricted.
mcq.fast: Under-consumed but good for society = merit good -> subsidise.

mcq.q: When the government fixes a maximum price for a good below its equilibrium price, the likely result is:
options: A shortage, and possibly black markets
A rise in the market price above equilibrium
mcq.explain: A price ceiling below equilibrium makes the good cheaper, so quantity demanded rises while quantity supplied falls, creating a shortage. Rationing, queues and black markets often follow. A price floor above equilibrium, such as a minimum support price, creates a surplus instead.
mcq.topic: Public goods and price intervention (non-market pricing)
mcq.fast: Ceiling below equilibrium = shortage; floor above = surplus.
